name: Cuxhaven
title: Cuxhaven UTM for Offshore Wind, Ro-Ro and Elbe Shipping
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging in Cuxhaven for offshore wind vessels, ro-ro ships, fishing vessels and ships at the Elbe anchorages: decks, tanks and piping.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement in Cuxhaven for Offshore Wind Vessels, Ro-Ro Ships and Elbe Traffic
intro: Cuxhaven sits where the Elbe meets the North Sea, at the start of the long river passage to Hamburg, and its port has made itself the German Offshore Industry Center while keeping ro-ro links to Britain and Scandinavia, a fishing port and the island services to Helgoland. Installation vessels, ro-ro ships and trawlers all lie here long enough for gauging. Atlantis keeps no one in Cuxhaven: the technicians fly in from India for each ship and work from the quay or, by launch, at anchor.

highlights.p: The offshore berths take jack-up installation vessels and heavy load transports serving wind farms in the German Bight. Between campaigns, leg wells, jack-house structure, crane pedestals and deck grillages can be gauged and crack-tested while the vessel lies alongside.

highlights.h: Ro-ro services across the North Sea
highlights.p: Ro-ro services from the Cuxport multi-purpose terminal link Cuxhaven with Great Britain, Scandinavia and the Baltic. Ships on these rotations call often and briefly, so ramp, main-deck and tank-top gauging is planned around a weekend stay or an overnight in port.

highlights.h: Ships waiting at the Elbe mouth
highlights.p: Ships waiting for a Hamburg berth, the right tide or new orders anchor at the mouth of the Elbe. A launch from Cuxhaven can put a team aboard for deck, air-pipe and accessible tank gauging, or a pre-purchase check, during hours the ship would otherwise spend idle.

port.h: Cuxhaven at the mouth of the Elbe
p: Cuxhaven stands at the tip of the Lower Saxony coast where the Elbe estuary opens into the German Bight, and every ship bound for Hamburg, Stade or Brunsbüttel passes close by. The port lines the riverbank for some distance: the Steubenhöft and Seebäderbrücke piers for large ocean-going ships, the Amerikahafen with cargo and ship-chandler quays, the Cuxport multi-purpose terminal with its ro-ro ramps, the offshore terminal and the German Offshore Industry Center with heavy-load berths, and the tide-free Neuer Fischereihafen. Niedersachsen Ports owns the port infrastructure. Because the town sits at the river mouth rather than up the river, ships here face open North Sea weather on one side and the strong tidal currents of the estuary on the other.

Offshore wind has reshaped the port. A turbine nacelle factory stands beside the offshore terminal, wind energy components made in the area are shipped worldwide, and the heavy-load berths take jack-up installation vessels and heavy transports, with further berths added for the industry. Wind farm operators base crew transfer and service vessels here for the German Bight. Ro-ro traffic carries vehicles, containers and breakbulk to Britain, Scandinavia and the Baltic. The fishing port handles trawlers with cold storage and processing behind the quays and serves as the supply base for Helgoland and Neuwerk, while passenger ships run out to Helgoland. Cruise ships use the river piers, and general cargo ships and smaller bulk carriers work at the Amerikahafen. Pilot boats, tugs and survey craft add to the daily movements off the town.

Gauging demand at Cuxhaven is therefore unusually mixed. Installation vessels come back from a season offshore with structure that has worked hard: legs and spudcans, leg wells, crane pedestals and the deck grillages that carry monopiles, transition pieces and turbine parts. Ro-ro ships need ramp and deck work fitted into a tight service. Fishing vessels and island supply ships are small, and many are decades old, with wasted plating in fish holds, tanks and the hull around the waterline. The weather window matters more here than in sheltered ports: north-westerly gales can stop launch work at the anchorage for days in autumn and winter, while the offshore season keeps installation vessels at sea in summer and brings them alongside in the quieter months.

facilities.h: Cuxhaven berths, anchorages and docking options
p: At the offshore terminal and the German Offshore Industry Center, gauging fits around mobilisation, demobilisation and port stays between projects. Jack-up vessels lying at the heavy-load berths can open tanks and voids under their own permit system, and their crane and leg structures are reachable from the deck. Ro-ro ships at the Cuxport ramps give shorter windows, usually overnight or at weekends. In the fishing port, trawlers between trips lie at quays unaffected by the tide, which makes access straightforward, and the Amerikahafen suits general cargo ships and coasters while they work cargo.

Ships at the Elbe anchorages are reached by a launch booked through the ship's agent, and work there depends on the sea state and the strong tidal stream in the estuary, so scopes at anchor are kept short and ordered by priority. For a docking, merchant ships from Cuxhaven generally go up the Elbe to the yards in Hamburg or across to Bremerhaven, and readings taken here can be passed to whichever yard the owner picks as an early steel estimate.
list: Offshore terminal and German Offshore Industry Center — leg well, crane pedestal and deck grillage gauging on jack-ups and installation vessels between campaigns.
Cuxport ro-ro ramps — main-deck, tank-top and ramp structure readings on ro-ro ships during weekend or overnight stays.
Neuer Fischereihafen — hull, fish hold and tank gauging on trawlers and island supply vessels at tide-free quays.
Amerikahafen quays — hold and deck measurements on general cargo ships and coasters while cargo is worked.
Elbe mouth anchorages — short launch-borne gauging and pre-purchase checks on ships waiting for Hamburg berths or orders.
Yards in Hamburg and Bremerhaven — where Cuxhaven ships usually dock, with readings from here used to plan steel.

context.h: Offshore class rules, port state control and North Sea conditions
p: Cuxhaven is a German port under the Paris MoU, where the Ship Safety Division of BG Verkehr carries out port state control. Most of the offshore fleet based here falls outside the ESP regime that governs tankers and bulk carriers, but self-elevating installation vessels have their own class survey requirements, and the legs, jacking systems and leg wells receive particular attention at renewal. Wind farm developers and installation contractors frequently want evidence of structural condition before chartering a vessel for a campaign, so gauging between seasons often serves a commercial check as well as a class survey.

European climate rules weigh on the ro-ro and short-sea fleet calling here. EU ETS has covered voyages to and from EU ports since 2024, and FuelEU Maritime has set fuel intensity targets since 2025, so owners of older ro-ro ships on North Sea routes are weighing new tonnage against running existing ships for another cycle. Ships arriving from outside the EU must also carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation. For fishing vessels and small island craft, flag and class surveys set the pace instead, but corrosion in fish holds and wet spaces makes periodic gauging just as necessary on them.

jobs.h: Thickness measurement jobs typical of Cuxhaven
jobs.p: Cuxhaven work tends to arrive in seasons. Installation vessels and offshore heavy transports come alongside between campaigns, often in winter, and owners use the port stay for structural gauging before the next contract. Ro-ro ships book work into weekends, fishing vessels between trips, and ships at the anchorage for the hours they wait. Scopes for the offshore fleet are longer and more detailed, with crack detection added where fatigue is suspected; the others are short and tightly focused. Each is agreed with the superintendent before the team leaves India, and readings are sent ashore daily, so the owner can line up repairs before the next sailing. Typical requests:
list: A jack-up installation vessel back from a monopile campaign: leg well and jack-house structure, crane pedestal and main deck gauging, with magnetic particle testing at pedestal and leg-well welds.
A ro-ro ship on a North Sea service during a weekend at Cuxport: trailer-lane deck plating, stern ramp and tank-top readings.
A heavy transport vessel between wind component shipments: deck plating and grillage foundations under the cargo area.
A trawler between trips in the fishing port: shell plating near the waterline, fish hold and fuel tank gauging before its flag survey.
A bulk carrier anchored at the Elbe mouth awaiting a Hamburg berth: deck, hatch coaming and air-pipe gauging by launch for the superintendent.

logistics: Hamburg Airport is the usual gateway, with Bremen Airport as an alternative, and Cuxhaven is linked to both by road and regional rail. The ship's agent arranges ISPS access to the Cuxport and offshore terminals, and offshore vessels normally run their own inductions as well. Launches to the anchorages are booked through the agent and depend on the weather. The technicians from India travel on Schengen visas, so offshore owners planning work between campaigns should share the expected port stay as early as they can.
vessels: Offshore service and crew transfer vessels

faqs.q: Can you gauge a jack-up vessel while it is alongside in Cuxhaven?
faqs.a: Yes. Jack-ups lying at the heavy-load berths between campaigns are among the best ships to gauge thoroughly, because tanks and voids can be opened without cargo pressure and the crane and leg structures are reachable from deck. We plan around the vessel's maintenance work and its permit system, and give priority to the leg wells, jack-houses, crane pedestals and deck areas that carry installation loads.

faqs.q: Is it possible to gauge a ship at anchor off Cuxhaven?
faqs.a: It is, by launch, when the sea state and the tidal stream allow safe boarding. The anchorages at the Elbe mouth are exposed to north-westerly weather, so jobs there are kept short and ordered by priority: deck plating, hatch coamings, air pipes and tanks the crew has prepared. If the weather closes in, the remaining scope can be completed later at the ship's berth up the river.

faqs.q: Where do ships calling at Cuxhaven go for dry-docking?
faqs.a: Usually up the Elbe to Hamburg or across to Bremerhaven, both of which have yards that dock commercial and offshore ships, or to another North Sea yard of the owner's choice. Gauging at Cuxhaven before the docking gives the yard a steel figure in advance, and our team can follow the ship to the yard if the programme needs completing in dock.

faqs.q: Do you work on fishing vessels in Cuxhaven?
faqs.a: Yes. Trawlers and other fishing vessels need the same steel checks as cargo ships, scaled to their size: shell plating, especially near the waterline and around the stern, fish holds, fuel and water tanks, and deck plating under the winches. The tide-free fishing port makes access easy, and we fit the work between fishing trips with the skipper and the owner.
